posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain point around AI explainability, position the 'auditability' problem as the real issue, not AI itself
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' moment is going to become the defining compliance horror story of this decade. It's not really an AI problem though — it's an auditability problem. Most analytics tools, AI or not, have never been great at showing their working. The question is whether the industry builds toward explainability or just keeps banning things until the next tool comes along.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the adoption wall after 18 months — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that the dashboard isn't the product, behaviour change is
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never really the hard part. The hard part is the moment someone quotes a number in a meeting, gets challenged on it, and can't explain where it came from — so they go back to the spreadsheet they can defend line by line. That's not a tool problem, that's a trust problem, and it takes a lot longer than 18 months to fix. What did your finance team actually say when you asked them why?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-KPI trap, add the 'fewer metrics requires more courage not less effort' insight
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is almost always a political problem dressed up as a measurement problem — everyone's work needs to be 'on the dashboard' or it doesn't count. The hard part isn't cutting to 5, it's the conversation you have to have to get there. Most teams skip it and just add another chart. What made it possible for you to actually push that through?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at a retail brand is engaging with a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing and add the insight that the tooling problem is actually a governance problem in disguise
posts.draft_comment: The '3 definitions of revenue' thing is almost universal — I've heard that exact sentence from so many teams it's almost a cliché at this point, except it's genuinely painful every time. The licence rollout gets blamed but the real issue is that nobody decided who gets to be right before the tools went out. Self-service works fine when there's a single agreed source underneath it — without that you're just democratising confusion. Who actually owned that call at Velocity, or did it never really get made?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as a security risk — validate the framing with a sharp operational detail, with a CEO at a 90-person data company watching
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think it gets said enough. A hallucinated number in a dashboard doesn't announce itself — it just looks like a number, gets screenshotted into a slide deck, and ends up in a board meeting. The 'treat outputs like inputs' parallel is the one that should be keeping data teams up at night. How many orgs do you think are actually doing that right now vs. just assuming the AI is probably fine?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the core pain with a specific observation, add the 'built for builders not buyers' insight
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is almost beside the point — the real cost is every time someone in ops or finance needs an answer and has to go back to the one person who built the thing. The 'self-service' label has been doing a lot of heavy lifting for years, covering up the fact that most tools were designed to impress in a demo, not survive contact with an actual Tuesday morning. Complexity got mistaken for capability. Who exactly were these platforms built for?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director surfacing a classic data governance pain point — validate that culture is part of it, but add the nuance that tooling choices either enable or prevent that cultural chaos
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, same dataset, three answers — that's not really a culture problem, it's a permissions and definition problem that culture gets blamed for. When the tool makes it too easy to apply your own filters without flagging the divergence, people will. Every time. The harder question isn't how do you change behaviour, it's why did the tool let this happen silently for a whole quarter?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director exposing the adoption gap in Copilot rollout — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' insight and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: That 12% stat is more honest than most companies would admit publicly. The shadow AI thing is the tell — people aren't avoiding AI, they're avoiding AI that requires them to already know the answer before they can ask the question. It's less a Copilot problem and more a 'what do I even need to know today' problem that no prompt box really solves.
